Squeeze clay, stretch a rubber band, push a ball harder to make it faster.

s3.headline: Measures forces and explores friction
points: Measures force with simple tools such as a spring balance (newton metre).
A toy car slows faster on carpet than on a smooth floor.

s4.headline: Analyses balanced and unbalanced forces
points: Predicts how an object moves from the forces acting on it.
Equal pulls in tug-of-war: no movement; a stronger pull moves the rope its way.

s5.headline: Links force, mass and acceleration
points: Understands a bigger force speeds an object up more, and a bigger mass speeds it up less.
The same push gets an empty cart moving faster than a loaded one.

s6.headline: Explains gravity, friction and air resistance
points: Tells mass (amount of matter, in kg) from weight (pull of gravity, in N) and handles several forces at once.
A parachute: air resistance pushes up, gravity pulls down.

s7.headline: Describes gravity as attraction
points: Explains that objects attract each other and that things fall toward Earth; in a vacuum all fall alike.
A feather and a hammer fall together on the Moon.

s8.headline: Calculates speed, moments and pressure
points: Calculates speed = distance ÷ time (100 m in 20 s is 5 m/s) and draws distance-time graphs.
Calculates moment = force × distance from the pivot, and pressure = force ÷ area.
Describes balanced and unbalanced forces and explains diffusion (particles spreading out).

s7.headline: Recognises signs of a reaction
points: Spots bubbles, a colour change or a precipitate (solid forming in a liquid).
Vinegar + baking soda fizzes; iron rusts to orange-brown.

s8.headline: Writes word equations
points: Tells endothermic (takes in heat) from exothermic (gives out heat) reactions and orders metals by reactivity.
Predicts displacement: iron + copper sulfate -> iron sulfate + copper.

s7.headline: Tests acids, alkalis and neutrals
points: Uses indicators (litmus, universal indicator) to sort solutions.
Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali; lemon juice is acidic, soap is alkaline.
Tests gases: a glowing splint relights in oxygen; lime water turns milky with CO₂.

s8.headline: Reads pH and uses reactivity series
points: Reads the pH scale: 0-6 acid, 7 neutral, 8-14 alkaline.
Predicts acid + metal reactions using the reactivity series (metals ranked by reactivity): magnesium fizzes in acid, copper does not.

s6.headline: Tells mass from weight
points: Understands mass (amount of matter) differs from weight (pull of gravity).
A 60 kg astronaut has the same mass on the Moon but weighs less.

s7.headline: Begins to explain density
points: Begins to understand density (how much mass is packed into a space).
Same-size blocks of wood and lead: lead is heavier because it is denser.

s8.headline: Calculates concentration and pressure
points: Calculates concentration of a solution (grams per litre): 20 g in 2 L is 10 g/L.
Understands pressure = force ÷ area, so a sharp knife cuts better.

s1.headline: Identifies sound sources
points: Names what makes a sound and knows ears let us hear.
Drum, bell and voice make sounds; ears pick them up.

s2.headline: Links vibrations to sound
points: Explores how vibrations make sound and how sound fades with distance.
A plucked rubber band shakes; a far-away voice is quieter.

s3.headline: Investigates pitch, volume and materials
points: Explores high and low pitch, loud and quiet volume, and how sound travels through different materials.
A short ruler end twangs at a higher pitch; sound is muffled through a wall.

s4.headline: Explores instruments and sound levels
points: Explores how instruments make sound and measures loudness with a sound metre.
A thinner guitar string gives a higher note; an app reads loudness in decibels (dB).

s5.headline: Creates and measures waves
points: Rope or spring waves: counts how many waves pass in 5 seconds.

s6.headline: Applies sound ideas to real life
points: Uses sound knowledge in real-world situations.
Earmuffs cut noise; carpets and curtains reduce echo in a classroom.

s7.headline: Explains sound as vibrations
points: Says sound needs a medium (material to travel through) and describes echoes.
No sound in space (vacuum); a shout toward a cliff comes back as an echo.

s8.headline: Describes sound wave properties
points: Understands sound wave properties and measures frequency (pitch) and amplitude (loudness).
Frequency is waves per second in hertz (Hz): 440 Hz is the note A.

s1.headline: Notices what sunlight does
points: Sees that sunlight lights up and warms things.
A sunny playground feels warmer than a shady one.

s2.headline: Names light sources and shadows
points: Tells what gives off light and knows a shadow forms where light is blocked.
Sun, lamp and flashlight give light; a hand in the beam makes a shadow.

s3.headline: Explains how shadows form
points: Sees that a shadow changes when the light moves.
Flashlight held low and to the side makes a long shadow; held overhead, a short one.

s4.headline: Sorts transparent and opaque materials
points: Tests which materials let light through and knows light travels in straight lines.
Window glass is transparent, wood is opaque; light cannot bend around a book.

s5.headline: Explains reflection and seeing
points: Knows light bounces off surfaces and enters the eye, which is how we see.
A mirror bounces a flashlight beam onto a wall; we see a book because light reflects off it.

s6.headline: Compares brightness of sun and stars
points: Notices that distance changes how bright a light looks and observes light patterns.
The sun is a star; it looks brightest because it is much closer.

s7.headline: Shows light reflecting off surfaces
points: Tells light sources from things that only reflect light.
Sun and lamp make light; the moon and a mirror only reflect it.

s8.headline: Explains reflection, refraction and colour
points: Uses the law of reflection (angle in = angle out) and knows light bends (refraction) in glass or water.
A prism splits white light into colours; a red apple reflects red and absorbs the rest.

s2.headline: Builds simple circuits
points: Connects a battery, wires and a bulb, with a switch.
Closing the switch lights the bulb; opening it turns the bulb off.

s3.headline: Tests magnetic materials
points: Finds which materials a magnet attracts and feels magnets push and pull.
A paper clip sticks, a plastic spoon does not; two magnets can push apart.

s4.headline: Builds complete circuits and electromagnets
points: Knows current flows only around a complete loop and explores electromagnets.
A gap in the wire stops the bulb; a coil of wire on a nail with a battery picks up paper clips.

s5.headline: Tests conductors; compares circuits
points: Finds which materials let electricity pass and compares series and parallel circuits.
Copper conducts, rubber insulates; bulbs in parallel stay brighter than in series.

s6.headline: Builds complex circuits safely
points: Builds multi-part circuits, follows electrical safety rules and names renewable energy sources.
Never touch sockets with wet hands; solar, wind and hydro power are renewable.

s7.headline: Explains basic magnetism
points: Sorts magnetic from non-magnetic materials and knows magnets have poles.
Iron and steel are magnetic; copper, aluminium and plastic are not.

s8.headline: Maps fields and builds electromagnets
points: Shows a magnetic field with iron filings or a compass and lists what makes an electromagnet stronger.
More coils, more current or an iron core; used in doorbells and scrapyard cranes.

s5.headline: Builds and tests simple circuits
points: Connects a battery, bulb and wires and checks that it works.
Bulb will not light: looks for a gap or loose wire.

s6.headline: Fixes circuits to solve problems
points: Changes a circuit to get a different result.
Adds a second battery for a brighter bulb; adds a switch to turn it off.

s7.headline: Builds and explains series circuits
points: Builds a series circuit, draws it with circuit symbols and explains current as electrons flowing.
Sorts conductors from insulators and predicts a bulb dims when another is added in series.

s8.headline: Explains current in series circuits
points: Describes in more detail how current flows around a single loop.
Current is the same at every point in a series circuit.

s1.headline: Notices day, night and seasons
points: Observes light and dark each day and how the year changes.
Summer days are warmer and lighter for longer than winter days.

s2.headline: Models the sun's path and shadows
points: Tracks how the sun seems to move across the sky and links day and night to Earth's spin.
A shadow stick is long in the morning and short at noon.

s3.headline: Tracks moon phases
points: Records the moon's changing shape and knows Earth's spin causes day and night.
The moon goes from thin crescent to full and back in about a month.

s4.headline: Analyses weather and climate
points: Finds weather patterns and compares climate in different regions.
A chart of daily rain and temperature; deserts are dry, rainforests are wet.

s5.headline: Models Earth's rotation
points: Shows how Earth's spin gives day and night.
Globe and flashlight: the lit side is day, the dark side is night.

s6.headline: Finds patterns in sky and seasons
points: Observes shadows, day and night and seasons and notices that they repeat.
Shadows are shortest at noon; days are longest in summer.

s7.headline: Describes the Earth-Sun-Moon system
points: Knows how Earth, Sun and Moon move in relation to each other.
Earth orbits the Sun in a year; the Moon orbits Earth in about a month.

s8.headline: Models eclipses and tides
points: Uses the Sun-Moon-Earth lineup to explain eclipses and the Moon's pull to explain tides.
Solar eclipse: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth.

s1.headline: Notices sunlight warms things
points: Feels that the sun heats surfaces.
A metal slide is warm after sitting in the sun.

s2.headline: Spots light, heat and movement energy
points: A lamp gives light, a heater gives heat, a rolling ball has movement.

s3.headline: Knows energy makes things happen
points: Understands that changes need energy.
A toy car needs a battery to move; a plant needs light to grow.

s4.headline: Links energy to moving objects
points: Sees that moving things have energy and that energy can change form.
A rolling ball has movement energy; rubbing hands turns movement into heat.

s5.headline: Shows energy transfer and change
points: Demonstrates energy moving between objects and changing form.
A battery powers a motor: stored energy → movement; a fan turns electricity into air movement.

s6.headline: Explains energy is conserved
points: Knows energy is not used up, only changed, often in several steps.
Power station: fuel → heat → steam movement → electricity → light in a home.

s7.headline: Shows energy changing form
points: Tracks energy as it changes and gives examples of energy 'lost' as heat.
A light bulb turns electricity into light plus wasted heat.

s8.headline: Tracks energy transformations
points: Keeps following energy through changes, in more detail.
Roller coaster: stored energy at the top → movement → heat from friction.

s1.headline: Asks questions about what they see
points: Wonders about things they notice.
Why does the ice melt in my hand?

s2.headline: Asks questions and suggests ways to answer
points: Asks a question and says how to find out.
Do plants grow better in light? Grow two plants and compare.

s3.headline: Makes predictions
points: Says what will happen using observations and what they already know.
I think ice melts faster in the sun because the sun is warm.

s4.headline: Defines problems; forms hypotheses
points: Picks a specific problem to investigate and states a hypothesis (a testable guess).
If the ramp is steeper, then the car will roll faster.

s5.headline: Predicts using science knowledge
points: Uses science ideas and patterns to predict outcomes.
Metal conducts heat, so a metal spoon will get hot faster than a wooden one.

s6.headline: Forms testable questions with reasons
points: Writes a question that can be tested and gives reasons for the hypothesis.
Does salt change how fast ice melts? Salt lowers the freezing point, so I think yes.

s7.headline: Asks testable questions
points: Tells a testable question or hypothesis from one that cannot be tested.
Testable: does temperature change how fast sugar dissolves? Not testable: is red the best colour?

s8.headline: Writes clear testable hypotheses
points: States how changing one thing will affect another and designs a test for it.
The warmer the water, the faster sugar dissolves; test at 20, 40 and 60 °C.

s1.headline: Answers questions by observing
points: Uses looking and watching to find answers.
Watch an ant trail to see what the ants carry.

s2.headline: Uses experience; suggests methods
points: Draws on firsthand experience and suggests ways to collect information.
How tall is the bean plant? Measure it every day.

s3.headline: Plans simple investigations with help
points: Which paper towel soaks up most? Pour one cup of water on each of three brands.

s4.headline: Designs fair tests
points: Decides what to measure and changes only one thing.
Same ramp, same car; measure how far it rolls on carpet and on wood.

s5.headline: Plans fair tests with one variable
points: Controls everything except one variable (the thing that changes).
Seeds with different amounts of water; same soil, light and seeds.

s6.headline: Designs full investigations
points: Plans a complete test and controls several variables.
Which soap makes the most foam? Keep water amount, temperature and stirring time the same.

s7.headline: Names variables, starts a procedure
points: Names what to change, what to measure and what to keep the same, then begins a method.
Change: amount of salt; measure: time to melt; keep same: ice size and temperature.

s8.headline: Designs fair tests with controls
points: Keeps other variables constant and chooses sensible measuring ranges and intervals.
Test water at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C, measuring every 10 degrees.

s1.headline: Observes to collect evidence
points: Looks closely and uses senses to gather facts.
The leaf is green, smooth and has veins.

s2.headline: Records observations; measures simply
points: Writes or draws what they see and takes simple measurements.
A leaf is 6 cubes long.

s3.headline: Measures with rulers and timers
points: Uses simple equipment correctly.
A pencil is 15 cm long; a ball rolls for 4 seconds.

s4.headline: Observes in order; measures several things
points: Observes in an organised way and measures more than one variable.
Each day, record plant height and the amount of water given.

s5.headline: Observes carefully; measures accurately
points: Looks for small details and reads tools at the right mark.
Reads 24 mL at eye level on a measuring cylinder; a thermometer reads 23 °C.

s6.headline: Chooses and uses tools correctly
points: Picks the right tool for the job and uses it properly.
Thermometer for temperature, balance for mass, measuring cylinder for volume.

s7.headline: Records observations with units
points: Notes useful details and writes measurements with correct units.

s8.headline: Measures accurately and precisely
points: Explains why careful measuring matters: accurate is close to the true value, precise is repeat readings that agree.
Readings of 20.1, 20.2 and 20.1 cm are precise.

s1.headline: Records work with pictures
points: Draws the stages of what they did.
Three pictures: seed, root, shoot.

s2.headline: Uses labelled drawings and simple tables
points: Labels drawings and fills in a simple table.
A plant drawing with 'leaf' and 'stem' labels; a table of day and height.

s3.headline: Presents results in charts and tables
points: Shows results as drawings, bar charts or tables.
A bar chart of how far three toy cars rolled.

s4.headline: Records data in several formats
points: Organises data in tables, charts and drawings in a tidy order.
A table with Day and Height (cm) columns, then a bar chart of the same data.

s5.headline: Makes data tables; picks graphs
points: Builds detailed tables and chooses a suitable graph.
Line graph for temperature over time; bar chart to compare groups.

s6.headline: Organises larger data sets
points: Uses more advanced displays for complex data.
A table of 5 trials per ramp height and a scatter graph of height against distance.

s7.headline: Organises data in standard formats
points: Puts data in simple tables and charts with headings and units.
Column headings: Temperature (°C), Time (s).

s8.headline: Makes tables before experimenting
points: Sets up the table first and picks a suitable way to record.
A blank table with trial 1, 2, 3 and average columns, ready before the test.

s1.headline: Makes simple comparisons
points: Says how things are the same or different.
The big ball bounces higher than the small ball.

s2.headline: Spots basic patterns
points: Notices things that go together.
Plants in more light are taller.

s3.headline: Finds patterns in results
points: Spots a pattern and states a simple rule.
The steeper the ramp, the farther the car rolls.

s4.headline: Identifies trends and outliers
points: Spots the overall direction and odd results (outliers) and suggests reasons.
Heights 5, 7, 9, 30 cm: the 30 is an outlier, maybe a measuring slip.

s5.headline: Analyses complex patterns; predicts
points: Studies patterns in more detail and uses them to predict.
Temperature rises 2 °C every minute, so expect about 10 °C more after 5 minutes.

s6.headline: Finds patterns and anomalies
points: Spots patterns and results that don't fit and uses basic statistics.
Finds the mean (average) of 5 trials and notes one far from the rest.

s7.headline: Finds patterns, spots unusual results
points: Looks over collected data for patterns and results that don't fit.
A spring stretches more with more mass, except one reading that is off.

s8.headline: Separates correlation from cause
points: Knows two things changing together does not prove one causes the other, and explains odd results.
Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause sunburn.

s1.headline: Compares results with predictions
points: Checks what happened against what they thought would happen.
I thought the boat would float, and it did.

s2.headline: Explains what happened
points: Looks back and says what happened and why.
The ice melted because the room was warm.

s3.headline: Draws conclusions using science ideas
points: Uses what they know to explain results.
The magnet picked up only things that contain iron.

s4.headline: Says what evidence shows
points: Explains what the data shows and judges whether it supports the prediction.
The car went farther on the smooth floor, which supports my prediction.

s5.headline: Builds explanations from evidence
points: Uses evidence to explain results and notes limits of the test.
Plant 1 grew taller, but we only tested one plant.

s6.headline: Draws justified conclusions
points: Backs conclusions with data, judges how reliable the results are and suggests improvements.
Repeat the test 5 times for more reliable results.

s7.headline: Begins evidence-based conclusions
points: Writes a conclusion that points to the data.
More salt melted ice faster: 10 g took 4 min, 20 g took 2 min.

s8.headline: Explains limits; suggests improvements
points: States what the conclusion cannot show and how to improve the investigation.
Only 3 temperatures were tested; test more and use a stopwatch.

s5.headline: Measures with five common tools
points: Measures volume, temperature, time, length and force.
Measuring cylinder (mL), thermometer (°C), stopwatch (s), ruler (cm), force metre (N).

s6.headline: Records measurements in tables and graphs
points: Water temperature each minute in a table, then a line graph.

s7.headline: Records measurements with correct units
points: Organises data in order and always writes units.
50 mL, 2.5 g, 12 s - not just the numbers.

s8.headline: Averages repeated measurements
points: Finds the mean of repeats, spots trends and draws suitable graphs.

s1.headline: Shares ideas by talking and drawing
points: Tells and draws what they found.
Draws a seed with a root and tells the class.

s2.headline: Explains findings aloud and with diagrams
points: Describes what happened using spoken words and a labelled picture.
A shadow diagram showing why the shadow grew longer.

s3.headline: Presents findings clearly
points: Tells others what they did and what they found.
Shows a chart and says, 'The red car went farthest.'

s4.headline: Writes simple reports with evidence
points: Includes what was done and what the results show.
We tested two soils. Soil B plants grew 8 cm; soil A plants grew 4 cm.

s5.headline: Presents detailed findings with data
points: Backs up findings with tables or graphs.
A poster with a bar chart of results and a one-line conclusion.

s6.headline: Explains complex ideas with science terms
points: Communicates clearly using scientific vocabulary.
Says 'evaporation' and 'condensation' instead of 'drying up' and 'getting wet'.

s7.headline: Begins using science vocabulary correctly
points: Uses science words in the right way.
Sugar dissolves in water; ice melts.

s8.headline: Presents findings clearly and fully
points: Gives the right amount of detail.
A report with aim, method, results table and conclusion.

s5.headline: Supports ideas with evidence
points: Starts backing up a claim with something observed.
This magnet is strong: it picked up 8 paper clips.

s6.headline: Backs arguments with data and models
points: Uses measurements and models to support a claim.
A temperature graph and a particle diagram show why hot water dissolves sugar faster.

s7.headline: Begins building science arguments
points: Makes a claim, gives evidence and explains why the evidence supports it.
Claim: metal conducts heat. Evidence: the spoon in hot water got hot. Reason: heat travels through metal.

s8.headline: Supports claims with specific evidence
points: Uses precise evidence, explains the limits of conclusions and compares results with predictions.
Sugar dissolved in 30 s at 60 °C and 90 s at 20 °C, but only two temperatures were tested.

s1.headline: Spots simple problems
points: Names a problem to solve.
The teddy keeps falling off the shelf.

s2.headline: Recognises problems needing solutions
points: Sees when something needs fixing.
The playground is too sunny, so it needs shade.

s3.headline: Asks questions about the problem
points: Asks what the solution must do.
For a toy-car bridge: how wide? how strong? which materials?

s4.headline: Sets criteria and constraints
points: Lists what a solution must do (criteria) and its limits (constraints).
Bridge must hold 5 toy cars (criteria) using only paper and tape (constraints).

s5.headline: Analyses complex problems; finds variables
points: Breaks a problem down and names the key things that affect it.
A cargo boat: hull shape, weight of cargo, material.

s6.headline: Breaks problems into parts
points: Splits a complex problem into smaller parts and weighs several factors.
Planning a school garden: sunlight, soil, water, cost, space.

s7.headline: Lists criteria and constraints
points: Recognises a problem needing a solution and lists what the solution needs and its limits.
Egg drop: egg must not crack (criteria); 3 sheets of paper and 20 cm of tape (constraints).

s8.headline: Defines problems with clear criteria
points: Phone holder: holds the phone at 45°, costs under $2, uses recycled card.

s1.headline: Solves problems with materials at hand
points: A cardboard tube and tape make a ramp for a toy car.

s2.headline: Designs simple devices
points: Plans and makes a simple device.
A shade structure for a toy; a sound maker from a tin and rubber bands.

s3.headline: Sketches and models ideas
points: A sketch of a kite, then a paper model.

s4.headline: Generates ideas, picks the best
points: Comes up with several ideas and chooses the best approach.
Sketches three bridge designs and picks one to test.

s5.headline: Designs devices for a function
points: Designs for a specific job, such as changing one kind of energy into another.
A waterwheel that turns water movement into a lifted weight.

s6.headline: Designs efficient, sustainable solutions
points: Considers efficiency and sustainability in more advanced designs.
A solar-powered phone charger built from recycled parts.

s7.headline: Brainstorms several solutions
points: Offers many ideas before choosing.
Keeping a drink cold: foil wrap, wet cloth, insulated sleeve, ice pack.

s8.headline: Researches and compares solutions
points: Looks at existing solutions and uses a decision matrix (a table scoring options against criteria).
Score three bike lights from 1 to 5 on cost, brightness and battery life.

s1.headline: Builds simple structures
points: Builds with blocks and other materials.
A tower made from blocks.

s2.headline: Builds and tests simple designs
points: Makes a design and checks whether it works.
Does the paper tower stay up when you blow on it?

s3.headline: Builds prototypes and tests them
points: Makes a first version (prototype) and tests whether it works.
A paper helicopter dropped from a chair to see if it spins.

s4.headline: Tests under different conditions
points: A shelter tested in wind (a fan) and in rain (a spray bottle).

s5.headline: Builds working prototypes; tests step by step
points: A parachute dropped 3 times from the same height, timing each fall.

s6.headline: Builds complex systems; tests thoroughly
points: Builds multi-part systems and plans full test routines.
A model lift with pulleys, tested with 3 loads, 3 times each.

s7.headline: Builds models; tests against criteria
points: Builds a simple prototype, checks it against the criteria and records what works.
Bridge must hold 10 coins but held 8, so it fails; record it.

s8.headline: Builds and tests several versions
points: Makes more than one version of a prototype and documents the design process.
Versions 1, 2 and 3 of a boat, each with photos, notes and test results.

s2.headline: Discusses improvements
points: Talks about how to make a design better.
The tower fell, so make the base wider.

s3.headline: Compares strengths and weaknesses
points: Says what is good and not so good about each solution.
A paper cup is light but gets soggy; a plastic cup stays dry.

s4.headline: Analyses results; finds improvements
points: Reads test results to decide what to change.
The boat sank with 12 marbles, so make the hull wider.

s5.headline: Refines designs through testing
points: Tests, improves and tests again.
Test 1: parachute falls in 2 s. Bigger canopy, test 2: 3 s.

s6.headline: Optimises through repeated improvement
points: Improves a design over several rounds and weighs costs against benefits.
A better material costs $3 more but lasts twice as long.

s7.headline: Compares strengths and weaknesses
points: Judges each solution's good and weak points.
A foam cup keeps heat best but is the least eco-friendly.

s8.headline: Evaluates designs against each criterion
points: Tests against every criterion, keeps the best features, combines them and makes trade-offs.
Take the strong joint from design A and the light frame from design B.

s1.headline: Uses models to show relationships
points: Uses a picture or object to show how things relate.
Arrows between pictures show a rabbit eating grass.

s2.headline: Makes simple physical models
points: Builds a model from everyday objects.
A clay volcano; a cardboard sun and Earth.

s3.headline: Uses models to explain ideas
points: Uses a model to show others how something works.
A flashlight and a ball show why the moon has phases.

s4.headline: Develops models to explain phenomena
points: Makes a model that explains something they see.
A bottle with a lid and warm water models the water cycle.

s5.headline: Models complex relationships
points: Builds models with many parts and shows how they link.
A food web with string joining eight organisms.

s6.headline: Designs models; knows their limits
points: Builds detailed models and understands what they leave out.
A model solar system is not to scale: real distances are far bigger.

s7.headline: Makes physical and diagram models
points: Makes models, draws diagrams of ideas and uses symbols or formulas.
A particle diagram of a gas; H₂O; speed = distance ÷ time.

s8.headline: Models invisible processes
points: Explains analogies as models, models unseen processes, judges strengths and weaknesses, and revises with evidence.
Water in pipes as electric current: helpful, but wires don't leak.

s1.headline: Writes simple sentences
points: Forms lowercase and capital letters correctly and joins some letters.
"The dog is big." with a capital and full stop; spells tricky words (said, was) correctly.

s2.headline: Writes sentences with correct punctuation
points: Uses capitals, periods, question marks and commas in lists, with neat, joined letters.
"We bought apples, pears, and plums."
Reads own writing aloud and proofreads for errors.
Milestone: Emergent writing is mastered by the end of ages 6–7; can write simple sentences independently.

s1.headline: Writes simple stories with drawings
points: Draws pictures and adds labels to tell a short story.
Draws a dog and a tree, labels them dog and park.

s3.headline: Develops characters, settings and plots
points: Adds relevant details and dialogue to stories.
"Lily crept into the cave. "Who's there?" she whispered."

s4.headline: Tells stories with beginning, middle, end
points: Adds interesting descriptions; also writes imaginative stories, poems and simple plays.
"One snowy morning, Tom found a tiny dragon."

s5.headline: Writes stories that make sense
points: Creates interesting characters, settings and events that fit together.
A girl on a windy beach follows her lost kite and finds it.

s6.headline: Writes engaging stories
points: Uses interesting characters, settings and events to keep readers hooked.
Ends a scene with a surprise: "The door creaked open by itself."

s7.headline: Uses dialogue, pacing and description
points: Builds characters and setting and orders events logically, using dialogue, pacing (speeding up or slowing down events) and sensory details.
"The kitchen smelled of burnt toast, and the smoke alarm screamed."

s8.headline: Writes complete, engaging stories
points: Writes strong openings, developed characters, a clear plot and a satisfying ending.
Opens with action or a question; ends with the hero changed by events.

s3.headline: Organises stories and information pieces
points: Facts about frogs grouped as what they eat and where they live.

s4.headline: Writes to teach with facts
points: Teaches others about a topic using facts and helpful details.
"Frogs lay eggs in water. The eggs hatch into tadpoles."

s5.headline: Writes to teach with facts
points: Teaches others about a topic using facts and details.
"Honeybees live in hives and make honey from nectar."

s6.headline: Writes information texts that explain
points: Teaches a topic using facts and clear explanations.
"Leaves change colour in fall because shorter days make the green chlorophyll fade, showing yellow and orange."

s7.headline: Writes informative texts with definitions
points: Examines a topic using facts, definitions, details and examples.
Defines "habitat" (a place where an animal lives), then gives a coral reef as an example.

s8.headline: Writes organised explanations
points: Explains a topic using facts, definitions, examples and clear organisation.
A volcano report defines magma, explains eruptions and gives Mount St. Helens as an example.

s3.headline: Writes organised opinions
points: "I think cats are the best pets. First, ... Last, ..."

s4.headline: Gives reasons for opinions
points: Supports their opinion with clear reasons and examples.
"I like our school garden because we grow food and learn about plants."

s5.headline: Supports opinions with reasons and facts
points: "Our library is open only 2 days a week, so it should open 5 days."

s6.headline: States views with good reasons
points: "Kids should wear bike helmets because a fall can cause a serious head injury."

s6.headline: Writes arguments with both sides
points: Presents both sides and convinces readers with logical points.
"Some think phones help learning; others find them distracting." Then explains why one view is stronger.

s7.headline: Writes arguments with claims and evidence
points: States a clear claim with reasons and relevant evidence, organised logically.
Claim: school should start later. Evidence: teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

s8.headline: Addresses opposing views
points: Writes a clear claim, acknowledges opposing views and uses logical evidence.
"Some say later starts hurt sports, but practices can move to the afternoon."

s4.headline: Writes poems, stories and plays
points: "Rain taps the window / like tiny drums."

s5.headline: Writes creatively in many forms
points: Writes poems, stories and plays, including directions for actors.
Play script: Mia (whispering): "Did you hear that?"

s6.headline: Writes in different styles
points: A funny rhyming poem vs a calm, unrhymed poem about the sea.

s7.headline: Writes in diverse forms
points: Writes arguments, informative texts and narratives.
A persuasive letter, a report on sharks and a short story.

s8.headline: Experiments with poetic forms
points: Writes poems trying different forms, imagery, rhythm and literary devices.
A haiku (5-7-5 syllables) with vivid images; personification: "The moon yawned."

s2.headline: Checks own writing
points: Reads own writing aloud and proofreads for errors.
Spots a missing period or fixes "frend" to friend.

s3.headline: Plans, revises and edits writing
points: Plans by recording main points and organising ideas, using graphic organisers (planning charts) and notes from texts.
Judges own and others' writing for sense, accuracy and effectiveness.
Revises and edits using proofreading strategies and digital tools.

s4.headline: Plans and improves writing
points: Thinks about main ideas before writing; fixes mistakes and makes changes with help from others.
Takes notes from sources and records where facts came from, like a book title.

s5.headline: Plans, drafts, revises and edits
points: Works through each step with help from classmates and teachers.
Plans with a web, writes a draft, swaps with a partner for feedback, then fixes it.

s6.headline: Plans and improves writing carefully
points: Plans a clear beginning, middle and end; revises, edits and tries new approaches.
Sketches a story map first, then rewrites a weak opening.

s7.headline: Uses planning and multiple drafts
points: Plans with brainstorming, graphic organisers or outlines; revises through several drafts and evaluates writing for effectiveness.
Takes notes in different ways and uses them in writing.
Writes regularly, both short and extended pieces.

s8.headline: Plans, revises and writes regularly
points: Plans by brainstorming, outlining or mapping ideas; revises for clarity, word choice, organisation and correctness.
Writes short pieces in one sitting and longer projects, like research over weeks.

s3.headline: Organises writing in paragraphs
points: Uses paragraphs and sections with clear beginnings and endings.
A new paragraph for each new idea: first food, then habitat.

s4.headline: Orders ideas in paragraphs
points: A frog report: paragraph 1 homes, paragraph 2 food, paragraph 3 life cycle.

s5.headline: Groups related ideas in paragraphs
points: All sentences about a dog's training in one paragraph, its feeding in another.

s6.headline: Guides readers with paragraphs and sections
points: Organises ideas so readers can follow the thinking.
Adds section headings such as "Where Bears Live".

s7.headline: Links ideas with headings and transitions
points: Uses organizational features (headings, transitions, formatting); introduces topics and ends with logical conclusions.
Transition: "In addition,"; conclusion that follows from the evidence.

s8.headline: Writes introduction, body and conclusion
points: Organises writing with a clear introduction, logical body paragraphs and strong conclusion.
Transition words: however, for example, as a result, in contrast.

s1.headline: Writes simple sentences
points: Writes a complete sentence with a capital letter and full stop.
"The cat sat on the rug."

s2.headline: Writes simple and compound sentences
points: Joins two ideas with and, but or so.
"I like soup, but it is hot."

s3.headline: Links ideas with time and joining words
points: Uses then, next, because and so; writes complete sentences that suit the task.
"We went outside because the rain stopped."

s4.headline: Writes longer connected sentences
points: Joins ideas with and, but, because, when, so, then, and links sentences with also, next, later, first, after that.
"First we mixed the batter. After that, we baked it."

s5.headline: Writes different types of sentences
points: Writes statements, questions and exclamations, and orders ideas with first, next and because.
"First we planted seeds. Will they grow?"

s6.headline: Connects ideas across paragraphs
points: Writes different sentence types, using joining and describing words, and transition words within and between paragraphs.
"Meanwhile, ..."; "For example, ..."

s7.headline: Varies sentence structure
points: Uses simple, compound and complex sentences for meaning and style, and builds detail with phrases and clauses.
"Although it rained, we played outside."; "The old dog, tired from the walk, slept."

s8.headline: Varies sentences for effect
points: Uses simple, compound and complex sentences for effect, and shapes sentences to add detail and shades of meaning.
"He waited. And waited. Finally, after what felt like hours, the door opened."

s5.headline: Changes style for different readers
points: Writes for different people and purposes, changing style as needed.
A chatty note to a friend; a polite letter to the principal.

s6.headline: Changes style and content for readers
points: Adjusts style and content to fit who will read it and why they are writing.
A silly poster for classmates; a serious request to the mayor.

s7.headline: Keeps appropriate style and tone
points: Keeps a formal or informal style and tone suited to task and audience, and develops a personal viewpoint and distinctive voice.
Formal: "I would like to request..."; informal: "Can we please...?"

s8.headline: Develops consistent voice and viewpoint
points: Keeps one clear voice and point of view that suits the writing purpose.
A serious tone in an editorial vs a humorous voice in a personal blog.

s2.headline: Uses descriptive words
points: Adds describing words and phrases to make writing clearer.
"a fluffy white rabbit" instead of "a rabbit".

s3.headline: Chooses interesting words
points: Swaps plain words for stronger ones.
rushed instead of went; gigantic instead of big.

s4.headline: Chooses specific, exciting words
points: Picks specific words that make writing clear and exciting.
walked -> marched; big -> enormous.

s5.headline: Chooses words to express feelings
points: Picks the best words to show ideas and feelings clearly.
upset -> heartbroken; happy -> thrilled.

s6.headline: Uses precise, descriptive language
points: Chooses exact words and description that create pictures in readers' minds.
"The soup was hot" -> "Steam curled off the bubbling soup."

s7.headline: Chooses precise, varied vocabulary
points: Matches word choice to purpose and audience.
Formal report: purchase; note to a friend: buy.

s8.headline: Chooses precise words, cuts wordiness
points: Uses exact, varied words for specific effects, and removes wordiness and repetition.
"Due to the fact that" -> "because"; "the sad, unhappy girl" -> "the sad girl".

s3.headline: Adapts writing to readers
points: Changes writing to fit different readers and purposes.
A thank-you note to Grandma vs a sign for the playground.

s4.headline: Writes for different people
points: Uses fitting language for friends, teachers and family.
"Hi Sam, want to come over?" vs "Dear Ms. Park, may I ask a question?"

s5.headline: Writes for different readers and purposes
points: Instructions for younger kids use simple words; a class report uses facts.

s6.headline: Fits content to readers and purpose
points: Changes style and content depending on who will read it and why they write.
Explains a game to a younger child in simple steps, to classmates with rules and strategy.

s7.headline: Creates content for audience and purpose
points: Task: persuade the principal -> a polite, reasoned letter with evidence.

s8.headline: Adjusts formality, vocabulary and tone
points: Writes for different audiences, adjusting formality, vocabulary and tone.
Text to a friend: "Thanks a ton!"; email to a teacher: "Thank you for your help."

s4.headline: Does simple research projects
points: Uses books and websites to learn about a topic and keeps track of sources.
Notes facts about penguins and writes the book title they came from.

s5.headline: Researches with several sources
points: Uses multiple sources, tracks where information comes from, and uses it to support writing.
Writes the book title or website name next to each fact.

s6.headline: Takes notes from several sources
points: Note card: "Octopus has 3 hearts" (Ocean Book, p. 12).

s7.headline: Researches and checks credibility
points: Does short projects with print and digital sources and judges how trustworthy they are.
Trusts a museum website over an unsigned forum post.
Paraphrases (rewrites in own words), quotes and cites sources to avoid plagiarism (copying).

s8.headline: Researches with credible sources
points: Takes organised notes from several credible sources and works the information in by paraphrasing, quoting and citing.
Puts ideas in own words and credits the source: "According to Lee (2024), reef coverage is shrinking."

s3.headline: Writes and shares using technology
points: Types, publishes and works with classmates on a writing project.
Class story typed together in a shared document.

s4.headline: Writes and shares on devices
points: Uses computers and tablets to write and work on writing with classmates.
Types a draft, then shares it for a partner's comments.

s5.headline: Uses digital tools to present writing
points: Writes, shares and presents work using computers.
Types a report and adds pictures for a slideshow.

s6.headline: Types and publishes for an audience
points: Types well enough to publish and work with others, and picks a good way to present for each audience.
Posts a class blog entry; builds a short slideshow.

s7.headline: Produces and publishes writing digitally
points: Uses technology to create, publish and co-write.
Co-writes in a shared document, then publishes an article online.

s8.headline: Drafts, revises and publishes digitally
points: Uses digital tools at every step of the writing process.
Drafts in a word processor, revises using classmates' comments, publishes to a class website.

s7.headline: Presents writing in suitable formats
points: Picks a layout and design that fit the writing.
Newsletter with a title and columns; letter in letter format.

s8.headline: Chooses format and presentation elements
points: Selects headings, graphics and fonts to suit the purpose.
Bold headings and a chart in a report; plain font for a formal letter.

s1.headline: Speaks in conversations and presentations
points: Builds spoken language through talk, discussion and short presentations.
Tells the class about a favourite toy.

s2.headline: Speaks fluently in varied settings
points: Keeps developing smooth, clear speech in different speaking situations.
Talks with a partner, then shares with the whole class.

s3.headline: Speaks in structured discussions
points: Sharpens spoken language in organised discussions and presentations.
Takes turns in a group talk, then presents a topic to the class.

s4.headline: Expresses ideas with richer language
points: Uses more varied vocabulary and longer sentences.
"The enormous dog barked because it was startled."

s5.headline: Speaks confidently in many contexts
points: Uses spoken language well in different situations.
Chats with friends, answers a teacher, tells a story to the class.

s6.headline: Fits spoken language to audience
points: Uses advanced words and phrasing suited to the listeners and purpose.
Explains a science idea to the class; chats casually at recess.

s7.headline: Speaks precisely and fluently
points: Gets ideas across clearly and smoothly with the audience in mind.
Picks exact words and adjusts for a younger child or an adult.

s8.headline: Masters spoken language in all contexts
points: Uses rich vocabulary and expression in any situation.
Debates a topic formally, then explains it simply to a friend.

s1.headline: Shares thoughts on stories and events
points: Says what they think and feel about a story or an event.
"The pig was funny because he fell in the mud."

s2.headline: Gives opinions about stories
points: Shares own thoughts about stories and personal experiences.
"My favourite part was the storm because it was loud."

s3.headline: Builds on others' ideas
points: Adds to what others say while sharing own thoughts clearly and politely.
"I agree with Mia, and I also think the wolf was lonely."

s4.headline: Shares ideas respectfully
points: States own thoughts while respecting different ideas from others.
"I see it differently. I think the fox was kind."

s5.headline: Joins group discussions
points: Listens to others and shares own ideas.
Waits for a turn, then adds: "I think it is because..."

s6.headline: Joins group discussions clearly
points: Listens to others and states own thoughts clearly.
"Ben said the dam broke. I think it was the rain, because..."

s7.headline: Engages actively in discussion
points: Listens closely, builds on others' ideas and states own views clearly.
"Building on Sam's point, I also think the author wants us to worry."

s8.headline: Weighs several viewpoints in discussion
points: Brings together different perspectives and adds meaningful points.
Sums up what two classmates said, then adds a new point.

s1.headline: Answers simple questions about texts
points: Responds to simple questions after hearing or reading a text.
"Who is the story about?" -> "A lost puppy."

s2.headline: Answers questions and explains thinking
points: Answers questions about texts and says why.
"Why was the girl sad?" -> "Her kite flew away."

s3.headline: Follows multi-step instructions
points: Listens carefully, responds suitably and carries out steps in order.
"Fold the paper, draw a circle, then colour it blue."

s4.headline: Asks questions when confused
points: Listens carefully and adds helpful comments to conversations.
"Can you say that again?"; "What does that word mean?"

s5.headline: Follows discussion rules, gives feedback
points: Asks when unsure and gives helpful feedback on speaking and presentations.
"I liked your clear voice. Can you explain the last step again?"

s6.headline: Asks and answers to learn more
points: Listens carefully, responds thoughtfully and clears up confusion with questions.
"Do you mean the first experiment or the second?"

s7.headline: Listens actively in discussions
points: Pays close attention and responds to what is said.
Takes notes, then asks a follow-up question.

s8.headline: Evaluates complex spoken texts
points: Listens closely to speeches and talks, judges the arguments and responds thoughtfully.
Hears a speech, spots a claim with no evidence and questions it.

s1.headline: Uses words for familiar topics
points: Pets: fur, paw, feed; "Once upon a time", "Can I have...?"

s2.headline: Uses time words and topic words
points: "First, we..."; "After lunch, I..."; "a shiny red apple".

s3.headline: Figures out words from sentence clues
points: Uses the words around a new word to guess its meaning.
"The frigid water made her shiver" -> frigid means very cold.

s4.headline: Uses nearby words and word parts
points: unhappy: un- means not, so "not happy".

s5.headline: Uses clues, word parts and tools
points: Figures out meanings from the story and known word parts; uses dictionaries for subject words.
rewrite = write again; looks up "habitat" in a science dictionary.

s6.headline: Learns word origins and subject words
points: Uses text clues and dictionaries, learns where words come from and uses subject words correctly.
astronaut comes from Greek words for star and sailor; "evaporate" in science.

s7.headline: Uses academic and subject vocabulary
points: Learns and uses age-level academic and subject-specific words.
"analyse" in English; "photosynthesis" in science.

s8.headline: Applies academic and subject terms
points: "infer" and "bias" in reading; "variable" in science.

s1.headline: Retells familiar stories
points: Includes the important information when retelling.
Goldilocks: tries three bowls, breaks a chair, runs away.

s2.headline: Retells with characters and settings
points: Retells a story and describes who is in it and where it happens.
"Little Red Riding Hood met a wolf in the forest."

s1.headline: Compares stories with own life
points: Shares thoughts and links stories to their own life or to other stories.
"Like Max, I was scared of the dark."

s2.headline: Explains thinking about texts
points: Says why they think something about a text.
"The wolf was mean because he blew the house down."

s3.headline: Builds on others' ideas
points: Adds to others' ideas while sharing own thoughts clearly and politely.
"I agree with Ana, and I think the boy was brave because he went back."

s4.headline: Shares detailed information and stories
points: Includes interesting details that listeners can follow.
"My dog is a fluffy brown terrier who digs holes in the garden."

s5.headline: Shares ideas in clear order
points: Puts ideas in order and backs them up with details.
"First, frogs lay eggs. Next, tadpoles hatch. The tadpoles have tails."

s6.headline: Shares facts using pictures and technology
points: Talk on volcanoes with facts and a slideshow photo.

s7.headline: States views and persuades
points: Shares own views clearly in discussion and gives persuasive speeches with reasons and evidence.
"School should start later: studies show students need more sleep."

s8.headline: Expresses complex ideas with support
points: Explains complex ideas and opinions with supporting details.
"Homework can help learning, but too much leaves no time to rest."

s1.headline: Answers simple questions about texts
points: "Where does the story happen?" -> "On a farm."

s2.headline: Answers questions about texts
points: "What did the boy find?" -> "A key under the mat."

s3.headline: Asks and answers to show understanding
points: Asks questions to check understanding and learn more.
"Why did the character leave?"; "What does that mean?"

s4.headline: Asks questions when confused
points: Listens carefully, asks when unsure and adds helpful comments.
"Can you say that again?"; "I'd add that..."

s5.headline: Follows rules and asks questions
points: Follows classroom discussion rules and asks when they do not understand.
Raises a hand, then asks "What does migration mean?"

s6.headline: Asks and answers to clarify
points: Asks and answers questions to learn more or clear up confusion.
"Do you mean the first map or the second?"

s3.headline: Takes part in group conversations
points: Follows discussion rules, takes turns, takes assigned roles and judges own and others' speaking and listening.
Group timekeeper; later says "I spoke clearly but too fast."

s4.headline: Builds on others in groups
points: Listens, shares ideas, builds on what others say and helps everyone take part.
"Jo, what do you think?"; "Adding to Sam's idea..."

s5.headline: Listens and shares in discussions
points: Listens to others, shares own ideas, follows discussion rules and asks when unsure.
Waits for a turn; asks "Can you explain that?"

s6.headline: Takes roles and includes others
points: Follows discussion rules, takes different roles and helps others join in.
Acts as note-taker or leader; asks "What do you think, Tia?"

s7.headline: Takes roles and keeps talks on goal
points: Helps a discussion reach its goal, respectfully notes agreement and disagreement, and gives constructive feedback on how well people communicated.
"I agree on cost, but I see the schedule differently."

s8.headline: Leads productive discussions
points: Guides the group, mediates differing viewpoints and helps solve problems together.
"You both want a quiet space; we could share time slots."

s3.headline: Reads aloud with expression
points: Matches pace, volume and punctuation; presents with details and visual aids; uses voice and movement in drama.
Pauses at a period, rises for a question mark; shows a life cycle poster.

s4.headline: Presents with expression and gestures
points: Reads stories and poems with expression that fits the meaning, uses body language and gives short presentations.
Reads a scary line in a low voice; shrugs for "I don't know".

s5.headline: Presents in order using media
points: Shares information in clear order with details, using pictures, videos and effects.
Volcano slides: what it is, how it erupts, a photo.

s6.headline: Gives confident presentations
points: Presents facts and details with pictures and technology to different groups, and picks the best layout.
Slideshow with a title slide, one clear chart and one image per idea.

s7.headline: Presents confidently with media
points: Uses suitable media, gives persuasive speeches with reasons and evidence, and uses voice, gestures and drama to bring out meaning.
Persuades the class to recycle using a chart; acts out a play scene.

s8.headline: Delivers polished presentations
points: Knows the content well, uses speaking techniques and keeps the audience engaged.
Opens with a question, varies tone, answers audience questions.

s3.headline: Adjusts speech to the situation
points: Uses speaking that fits the setting and changes how they talk for different listeners.
Louder voice for a presentation, quieter in a small group.

s4.headline: Speaks clearly for different listeners
points: Speaks clearly and confidently, changing how they talk for different people and situations.
"Hi, Grandma!" vs "Good morning, Mr. Lee."

s5.headline: Changes speech for the listener
points: Talks differently to friends than to adults.
"Wanna play?" to a friend; "May I go to the library?" to a teacher.

s6.headline: Adjusts talk to listener and situation
points: Changes how they speak for different people and situations.
Chats casually at recess; speaks formally when presenting.

s7.headline: Adapts pace, tone and volume
points: Changes speaking style for different audiences and purposes.
Slower and louder for a big crowd; softer and warmer to comfort a friend.

s8.headline: Adapts speech to audience and purpose
points: Chooses formal or informal language to suit the context.
"Hey, thanks!" to a classmate; "Thank you for your time" to a guest speaker.

s1.headline: Forms letters correctly
points: Writes lowercase and uppercase letters correctly and joins some letters.
Writes "Dan" with a capital D; joins the letters in "at".

s2.headline: Forms and joins letters neatly
points: Joins the letters in "jumping" with even size and spacing.

s3.headline: Writes legibly and fluently
points: Writes clearly at a speed that suits the task.
Quick, neat writing for notes; slower, careful writing for a poster.
Milestone: Letter formation and handwriting are mastered by the end of ages 7–8.

s1.headline: Spells familiar and common words
points: Spells common words, including tricky ones, and chooses sensible letters for sounds in new words.
Spells "said" and "the"; writes "train" as "trane" (sounds right).

s2.headline: Spells words with prefixes and suffixes
points: Spells regular and exception words correctly, including homophones (sound-alike words).
unhappy, playing; there/their.

s3.headline: Spells using patterns and word parts
points: to/too/two, there/their, jumping/jumped.

s4.headline: Spells with rules and homophones
points: Spells age-level words and applies patterns and rules consistently, including when adding suffixes.
hop -> hopping (double the p); make -> making (drop the e); to/too/two.

s5.headline: Spells age-level words with rules
points: Uses spelling patterns and rules.
happy -> happier (y changes to i); receive (i before e, except after c).

s6.headline: Spells using word parts and rules
points: Uses word parts, patterns and rules, including tricky sound-alike words.
their/there/they're; its/it's; unbelievable.

s7.headline: Spells with roots, prefixes and suffixes
points: Uses known patterns and word families, and checks spelling with dictionaries and spell-check.
tele- (far) in telephone, television; looks up "necessary".

s8.headline: Spells complex, unfamiliar words
points: Uses patterns, word roots and strategies to spell hard words.
bio (life) + logy (study) -> biology; phenomenon.

s1.headline: Explores nouns and verbs
points: Notices naming words and action words in texts.
"The dog runs": dog is a noun, runs is a verb.

s2.headline: Identifies nouns, pronouns, adjectives
points: Finds each of these in texts.
"She has a red hat": She is a pronoun, red an adjective, hat a noun.

s3.headline: Identifies and uses parts of speech
points: "The happy girl jumped": girl is a noun, happy an adjective, jumped a verb.

s4.headline: Uses naming, action, describing words
points: "The small cat jumped."

s5.headline: Uses comparing words correctly
points: big, bigger, biggest; good, better, best.

s6.headline: Uses all parts of speech
points: Uses conjunctions, prepositions and interjections correctly along with other word types.
"Wow! The cat sat under the table and purred."

s7.headline: Uses pronouns clearly
points: Uses pronouns correctly and spots and fixes unclear pronoun references.
"Tom told Ben he lost" (who lost?) -> "Tom told Ben, 'You lost.'"

s8.headline: Explains the job of each word type
points: Shows how each part of speech functions in a sentence.
In "She quietly closed the door", quietly is an adverb telling how she closed it.

s1.headline: Identifies sentences and statements
points: Spots sentences in texts and understands verbs and word order in statements.
"The cat sat." is a sentence; "Sat cat the" is not.

s2.headline: Writes statements, commands, questions
points: Recognises and writes all three, and writes simple and compound sentences.
"Come here." "Where is it?" "It rained, but we played outside."

s3.headline: Writes varied sentences with joining words
points: Writes different kinds of sentences and joins ideas with connecting words, in complete sentences.
"I was cold, so I wore my coat."

s4.headline: Writes the four sentence types
points: Writes telling, asking, commanding and exclaiming sentences with correct punctuation, and longer sentences with simple joining words.
"The sun is hot." "Is it hot?" "Drink water." "It is so hot!"

s5.headline: Writes varied, connected sentences
points: Writes different types of sentences linked with and, but, because.
"I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed."

s6.headline: Writes varied sentences clearly
points: Writes different sentence types and joins ideas with joining words and describing words.
"The tired hikers rested because the path was steep."

s7.headline: Uses simple, compound, complex sentences
points: Varies sentence structure for meaning and style and adds detail with phrases and clauses.
Simple: "We ran." Complex: "Because it rained, we ran home."

s8.headline: Builds and varies sentence types
points: Chooses structures for clarity and effect and uses phrases and clauses correctly, avoiding misplaced or dangling modifiers.
"Walking to school, the rain soaked me" -> "Walking to school, I got soaked by the rain."

s1.headline: Joins ideas with "and"
points: Uses "and" to join words and parts of sentences.
"cats and dogs"; "I ran and I jumped."

s2.headline: Uses because, if, when
points: Joins ideas with connecting words.
"I took an umbrella because it was raining." "If it rains, we stay in."

s3.headline: Uses correct grammar in speech and writing
points: Keeps verb tense and subject-verb agreement correct.
"I walked" not "I walk yesterday"; "The dogs are" not "The dogs is".

s4.headline: Matches subjects and verbs
points: Makes sure sentences make sense by agreeing subject and verb.
"She runs" not "She run"; "They play" not "They plays".

s5.headline: Uses past, present, future tenses
points: Uses correct grammar across tenses.
"I walked"; "I walk"; "I will walk".

s6.headline: Controls verb tenses and voice
points: Forms verb tenses correctly, matches subject and verb, and uses active and passive voice appropriately.
Active: "The dog chased the cat." Passive: "The cat was chased by the dog."

s7.headline: Uses standard English grammar consistently
points: "She doesn't know" not "She don't know"; "He and I went" not "Him and me went".

s8.headline: Applies grammar rules accurately
points: Uses correct verb tenses, pronoun agreement and subject-verb agreement.
"The team won its game"; "Neither of the boys is here."

s1.headline: Uses capitals and periods
points: Uses capital letters for "I", names and sentence starts, and rereads to check capitals and periods.
"Today I saw Mia at the park."

s2.headline: Uses capitals, periods, question marks
points: Also uses commas in lists.
"Where is Tom?" "I bought apples, pears, and plums."

s3.headline: Uses basic punctuation correctly
points: Uses periods, question marks, quotation marks and commas.
Mia said, "I am ready."

s4.headline: Uses commas, apostrophes, dialogue marks
points: Punctuates accurately for clarity and meaning.
don't; Sam's hat; "Look out!" she yelled.

s5.headline: Punctuates dialogue and writing correctly
points: Uses correct punctuation and capitals throughout, including when characters speak.
Mum said, "Dinner is ready."

s6.headline: Uses commas, quotation marks, colons
points: Chooses punctuation to keep writing clear, including colons and dashes.
"You need three things: a pencil, paper, and an eraser."

s7.headline: Punctuates for effect and clarity
points: Uses periods, commas, apostrophes and quotation marks for meaning, plus colons, semicolons, dashes, ellipses and hyphens.
Semicolon: "It was late; we went home." Ellipsis: "Wait..."

s8.headline: Punctuates to shape meaning
points: Uses commas, semicolons, dashes, colons and apostrophes to sharpen meaning, and commas between coordinate adjectives.
"a long, winding road" (comma) but "a big red barn" (no comma).

s1.headline: Uses "the" and "a/an"
points: Uses articles appropriately.
"an apple", "a pear", "the sun".

s2.headline: Uses plurals, verb endings, comparing words
points: mouse -> mice; walk, walks, walked, walking; tall, taller, tallest.

s3.headline: Uses correct grammar in speech and writing
points: Applies grammar rules when talking and writing.
"We went to the park" not "We goed to the park".

s4.headline: Matches subjects and verbs
points: Checks that sentences make sense by agreeing subject and verb.
"The birds sing" not "The birds sings".

s5.headline: Uses tenses and comparing words
points: "Yesterday I played, today I play, tomorrow I will play"; fast, faster, fastest.

s6.headline: Uses English grammar rules accurately
points: Follows grammar and language rules in writing and speaking.
"Ana and I are going" not "Me and Ana is going".

s7.headline: Uses standard English consistently
points: "We were late" not "We was late"; "I don't have any" not "I don't have none".

s8.headline: Keeps standard English accurate
points: Maintains standard English grammar across all writing.
"between you and me"; "fewer apples, less water".

s1.headline: Starts using set phrases
points: "Once upon a time", "Can I have...?", "Thank you".

s2.headline: Alphabetises words, uses time words
points: Puts words in ABC order by first letter and begins sentences with time words.
ant, bus, cat; "Later, we ate."

s3.headline: Matches language to context
points: Uses language that suits the situation.
"Hi!" to a friend; "Good morning, Mrs. Lee" to a teacher.

s4.headline: Uses synonyms to avoid repetition
points: Finds and uses words with similar meanings.
big -> huge, large; said -> whispered.

s5.headline: Chooses best words with tools
points: Picks words that express ideas and feelings clearly, using dictionaries and other tools.
sad -> gloomy; looks up a word in a thesaurus.

s6.headline: Picks words and punctuation for effect
points: Chooses words and punctuation for specific effects and uses formal or informal language to fit the situation.
"Stop!" for urgency; "Dear Mr. Lee" vs "Hey Sam".

s7.headline: Tells formal from informal language
points: Uses each appropriately and comments on non-standard English in texts.
"Hello, sir" vs "Hey, dude"; a character's "ain't" is non-standard.

s8.headline: Varies formality by purpose
points: Matches formality to the writing context and uses informal language on purpose for style.
Report: "The results were unexpected." Dialogue: "Wow, didn't see that coming!"

s2.headline: Rereads and proofreads own writing
points: Reads writing aloud and checks for errors.
Hears a missing word and adds it; fixes a capital letter.

s3.headline: Evaluates and revises writing
points: Judges own and others' writing for sense, accuracy and effectiveness, then revises and edits using proofreading strategies and digital tools.
Reads each sentence aloud to check it makes sense; runs spell-check.

s4.headline: Improves writing with feedback
points: Makes changes and fixes mistakes with help from others.
Writes two versions of a story scene; uses a book example to support an idea.

s5.headline: Plans, writes, revises, edits
points: Works through the writing steps with help from classmates and teachers.
A partner says "add more detail here"; the writer revises and fixes spelling.

s6.headline: Improves writing through the process
points: Plans, revises, edits and tries new approaches.
Rewrites a weak opening a new way; edits commas.

s7.headline: Strengthens writing over several drafts
points: Revises and edits multiple drafts and evaluates own and others' writing.
Draft 2 adds evidence; draft 3 cuts repeated sentences and fixes errors.

s8.headline: Revises for clarity and correctness
points: Improves clarity, word choice, organisation and correctness.
"very big" -> "enormous"; reorders paragraphs; fixes comma errors.
